59cd4e3d3c:
This chapter has two jobs. First, you build something real: a small command-line task tracker. It pulls together functions, classes, dataclasses, type hints, exceptions, file handling, and tests in one program you can actually run.

Second, it closes the guide with a glossary, a map of how the big ideas connect, a review plan, interview questions, and a checklist proving every promised topic got covered.
5e94769905: tasktracker is a program that manages a to-do list from the terminal. It has four commands: add, list, done, remove. Tasks persist in a JSON file between runs.
49c6142040:
It is deliberately small. There's no web framework, no database, and no third-party packages. It's stdlib only, so it runs anywhere Python 3.13 runs with zero installation.

The point is not the app. The point is seeing every major idea from this guide working together in one honest program. A dataclass holds the data. Functions do the work. Exceptions mark the failure modes. pathlib and json handle persistence. argparse draws the CLI boundary. unittest proves it all works.
ccc6c44ec5: Two files is a decision, not laziness. This program has one data type, one storage format, and four operations. Splitting it into packages, modules, and abstract base classes would teach the wrong lesson: that every program needs architecture. Architecture earns its keep when a program has competing pressures, such as multiple storage backends, plugins, or teams. Here it would just be distance between you and the code.
d382cd34c3:
A task is plain data with a fixed set of fields: an id, a title, a done flag, and a creation timestamp. That description is exactly what a dataclass is for. Write the fields with annotations, and the decorator generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ for you. The generated __eq__ compares field by field, which the round-trip test relies on.

(In 3.13 the generated __eq__ compares each field individually rather than packing them into tuples. The result is the same for well-behaved fields; see the sources.)
9554b6a4f8:
Two details deserve attention. First, created uses default_factory, not a plain default. A plain default like created: str = datetime.now(...) would call now() once, when the class body executes. Every task would get the same time stamp. default_factory calls the lambda fresh for each new task.

This is the same family as the mutable-default-argument bug from Chapter 2. Defaults are evaluated once, at definition time.
2d59fc9dd1: Second, the timestamp is timezone-aware (timezone.utc). A naive datetime silently means "local time, probably." Mixing naive and aware datetimes raises TypeError on comparison. Aware is the safer habit, because it removes an entire class of silent bugs.
86438c56d3: The dataclass also carries the JSON conversions, to_dict and from_dict. JSON is the boundary format. The conversions live with the data type, so the rest of the program never touches raw dicts. from_dict validates. A corrupt record raises StoreError, chained with from exc so the traceback keeps the original cause.
6c3d3280c8: load_tasks reads the JSON file and rebuilds Task objects. A missing file is not an error. It means "no tasks yet," so the function returns an empty list. Corrupt JSON, a non-list document, or an OS error becomes StoreError, with a message naming the file and the problem. save_tasks writes the list back as indented JSON, creating parent directories if needed.
38cc838fdc:
Why functions and not a TaskStore class? A class earns its place in three situations. It carries state between calls, manages a lifecycle (open connection, transaction), or offers polymorphism (swap backends). This storage does none of that. Each call is independent: path in, tasks out.

A class here would be a namespace with an __init__ that stores the path. That's ceremony: a layer of indirection without added meaning. Two module-level functions say exactly what happens. If the program ever grew a second backend, that would be the moment to reach for a class or a protocol.
4c0b4ae656: The operations are pure functions over a list of tasks: add_task, find_task, complete_task, remove_task, plus next_id. They take no paths, print nothing, and exit nowhere. That purity makes them trivially testable. A test builds a list, calls a function, and asserts on the result.
dd8ed2ba20:
Failures are raised, not returned.

  • find_task raises TaskNotFoundError for an unknown id.
  • add_task raises TaskTrackerError for a blank title.
  • load_tasks/save_tasks raise StoreError.

That's three exception types in one small hierarchy rooted at TaskTrackerError. Each carries a message already phrased for a human.
f8f9e96ff4: Raise at the point of failure and catch at the boundary: that is the whole error-handling design. The domain layer reports what went wrong. It never decides how the user should hear about it. That decision lives in exactly one place, main().
82c435cb20: argparse defines the four subcommands. main(argv=None) is the only function that touches the outside world. It parses arguments, loads tasks, dispatches to the domain functions, saves, and prints. The try block wraps all of it. The single except TaskTrackerError converts any domain or storage failure into a one-line stderr message and exit code 1.
51adb0be54:
This is the CLI boundary pattern: parse at the edge, raise in the middle, catch at the edge. One catch site means error formatting can't drift between commands.

Note what is not caught: KeyboardInterrupt, MemoryError, bugs in our own code. Catching everything would hide real failures. This is the "avoid hiding failures" rule from the errors chapter, applied.
fc745bbfbe: main returns an int instead of calling sys.exit itself, and it takes argv as a parameter. Both choices are for tests. A test can call main(["add", "x"]), capture stdout, and assert on the exit code without spawning a process. The if __name__ == "__main__": block at the bottom is the only place that talks to the real process.
fb6865d0e3: The store location comes from the TASKTRACKER_STORE environment variable, defaulting to ~/.tasktracker.json. The env override lets tests and examples point at a temp directory instead of touching your real home directory. That is also why every example below sets it.
72dc50b4b4: Here is tasktracker.py in full. It is also saved at code/ch08/tasktracker.py. Run that copy; don't retype it.
a6723d0504: Here is tests/test_tasktracker.py in full, saved at code/ch08/tests/test_tasktracker.py. It has sixteen tests across three layers: domain operations, storage, and the CLI boundary.
5e9a30d046:
A few test-design notes.

  • setUp gives every test a fresh temp directory and points TASKTRACKER_STORE at it. Tests never touch your real home directory and never interfere with each other.
  • The run_main helper is the payoff of main(argv) returning an int. The CLI gets tested like any other function, with stdout and stderr captured.
  • The exception tests use assertRaises as a context manager, the standard way to test that the right failure happens.
  • test_save_and_load_round_trip leans on the dataclass-generated __eq__. If to_dict/from_dict drop or mangle a field, the lists won't compare equal.
475b36656d: Every command below was executed on CPython 3.13.16 against a temp store. Set the same variable and your output will match. The exception is the created timestamps, which reflect when you run it.
99b55a08bb: The program is finished but not done. A good codebase invites its next change. Each of these is a half-hour exercise that reuses a chapter of this guide:
27f6a05d31:
Everything starts with functions. In Python a function is an object like any other: you can pass it, return it, and store it.

A closure is what you get when a function refuses to forget. It's an inner function that keeps referencing its enclosing scope's variables after the outer function has returned. That remembered scope is the mechanism behind most decorators.

A decorator is a callable that takes a function and returns a new one. The standard way to build it is a closure. The outer call captures the decorator's arguments, the middle takes the function, and the inner wrapper runs before or after it. So functions, closures, and decorators are one lineage. Each chapter-2 idea grows directly out of the previous one.
cafd2cafee:
Descriptors look unrelated until you see where they live: inside attribute access. Any object with __get__ (and optionally __set__/__delete__) can intercept obj.attr when placed as a class attribute. property is the descriptor you already know. It's a data descriptor that runs a method on access.

Plain functions are non-data descriptors. That's the quiet reason methods receive self without being asked. Accessing a function through an instance triggers its __get__, which binds the instance as the first argument. So descriptors are the machinery under classes, properties, and methods alike. The chapter-3 idea explains chapter-4 behavior you had been taking on faith.
6181bd276f:
Type hints are the thread running through the typing chapters. An annotation is inert at runtime; the interpreter stores it and moves on. But two different readers care about it.

Static checkers read hints to catch type errors before the program runs. And dataclasses read hints at class-creation time. The @dataclass decorator scans a class's annotations and generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ from them. A dataclass is literally a class decorator powered by type hints. The chapter-5 idea is chapters 3 and 6 combined.
54626b6c2e:
TypedDict and Protocol are pure typing constructs. They exist for the checker and vanish at runtime. A TypedDict declares the shape of a dict (key names and value types) with no validation when the program runs. A Protocol declares a structural interface. Any class having the right members satisfies it, with no inheritance needed.

Both answer one question: how do I describe this precisely to a reader and a checker without changing runtime behavior? Classes are the things being described. Hints, TypedDicts, and Protocols are the descriptions.
73319464da:
Day 2 — close the book and rebuild the small things. From memory, write three things:

  • a decorator with arguments (the three-level version)
  • a closure that demonstrates late binding, plus its fix
  • the Task dataclass with to_dict/from_dict

Then run them. Whatever you can't reproduce is what you didn't actually learn, so reread just those sections. Redo the Chapter 2 mutable-default exercise and the Chapter 7 generator-exhaustion exercise. Twenty minutes is enough; the point is retrieval, not rereading.
f119e7f847:
Week 1 — rebuild the capstone without looking. Delete your copy (keep the tests). Rewrite tasktracker.py from the spec: four commands, JSON persistence, the three exception types, errors caught only in main. Then run the original test file against your rewrite. Failing tests will point at exactly the design decisions you forgot, usually the exception boundary or default_factory.

Also explain MRO aloud in under two minutes. Then whiteboard the descriptor lookup path for obj.attr (instance dict → class → MRO → descriptor protocol). If you can't say it simply, you don't own it yet.
c371415d26:
Week 4 — perform under mild pressure. Set a timer for 30 minutes. From scratch, write a context manager (both the class form and the @contextmanager form) and a generator pipeline with yield from. Then answer ten interview questions from the next section aloud, as if someone asked.

Finish by building one capstone extension from the "Where to go next" list. Pick the atomic-write one. It is the best test of whether the reliability ideas stuck. It forces you to think about what happens when the program dies halfway through a save.
707c13dc81: 1. After a = []; b = a; b.append(1), what is a? Why? a is [1]. Assignment never copies; it binds a name to an object. b = a makes both names point at the same list, so mutating through b is visible through a. If you needed independence, you'd copy explicitly (b = a.copy() or list(a)).
2dafb66fb5: 2. When should you use is instead of ==? == asks "equal value" (via __eq__); is asks "same object." Use is only for singletons like None. x is None is the idiom because there is exactly one None. Using is for value comparison (like x is 1000) sometimes works by accident, due to CPython caching small ints. That caching is an implementation detail, not a promise.
c5fa950d11: 3. Why does def f(items=[]) accumulate items across calls? Default arguments are evaluated once, when the def executes, not per call. The same list object is reused as the default every time. The fix is the sentinel pattern: def f(items=None): items = [] if items is None else items. The root cause matches the dataclass default_factory lesson: definition-time evaluation.
3af962e7de: The lambdas close over the variable i, not its value at creation time. This is late binding. By the time they run, the loop has finished and i is 4. The fix is to bind the value as a default, lambda i=i: i, because defaults are evaluated at definition time.
9d6843005d: 5. What does @timer do to a function, mechanically? It's assignment: f = timer(f). timer receives the original function object and returns a new callable, usually a closure wrapping it. The name f is then rebound to the wrapper. That's why decorators can change behavior transparently. It's also why forgetting functools.wraps loses the original's name and docstring.
60d9d0b415: 6. Why does a decorator with arguments need three levels of nesting? @retry(times=3) must first produce a decorator, and then that decorator wraps the function. So the outer function takes times and returns the decorator. The decorator takes func and returns the wrapper. The wrapper takes the call's arguments. Each level exists because each call happens at a different time: decoration time, then call time.
5fd974dc27: 7. When is writing a raw descriptor better than using @property? When the same attribute logic must be reused across many classes or many attributes. A property is defined per class per attribute. A descriptor class (like a Validated or Typed descriptor) is written once and dropped into any class as a class attribute. If it's one attribute on one class, property is simpler. That's the whole decision.
a6e64092c6: 8. Why do methods automatically receive self? Functions are non-data descriptors: they define __get__ but not __set__. When you access obj.method, the descriptor protocol calls function.__get__(obj, type(obj)). That returns a bound method with obj pre-filled as the first argument. self isn't magic syntax. It's the descriptor protocol doing its job.
c2276e0e50: 9. In a diamond inheritance (D(B, C), both inherit A), which parent's method wins, and why is the answer predictable? Python linearizes the hierarchy with C3 into one MRO: D, B, C, A, object. Attribute lookup walks that single chain in order, so B's method wins over C's and A's. The answer is predictable because of two C3 guarantees. Every class appears after its subclasses, and local declaration order is preserved. super() follows this same chain.
0f1ca7ebca: 10. You define __eq__ on a class and suddenly instances can't be dict keys. What happened? Defining __eq__ without __hash__ makes Python set __hash__ to None. The class becomes unhashable. The rule is that equal objects must hash equal, and a mutable object with value-based equality can't promise a stable hash. If you need hashing, use @dataclass(frozen=True), which generates both consistently. Or define __hash__ deliberately.
1620bcf8d6: 11. What does frozen=True on a dataclass actually guarantee? It blocks attribute reassignment (obj.x = 1 raises FrozenInstanceError). It does not freeze the contents of mutable fields. A frozen dataclass holding a list can still have that list mutated. Frozen means "can't rebind fields," not "deeply immutable."
6f0d78531f: 12. You annotate a function to take a TypedDict and pass a dict with a wrong value type. What happens at runtime? Nothing. TypedDict is purely static. At runtime the annotation is ignored and the value is a plain dict. There's no validation and no error. If you need runtime validation, you build it yourself (or use a library). TypedDict was never that tool.
8fdebe7888: 13. What's the practical difference between annotating a parameter Any and object? Any tells the checker to stop checking: any operation is allowed, with no errors ever. object tells the truth: "I know nothing about this." So the checker forces you to narrow it (usually with isinstance) before doing anything specific. Any is convenient and contagious; object is honest.
713d65ff21: 14. Why does the type checker accept x + 1 after if isinstance(x, int) when x was str | int? Narrowing. isinstance is one of the constructs checkers understand. Inside the if branch, the declared union is narrowed to int, so the operation type-checks. In the else branch it's narrowed to str. The annotation didn't change. The checker's knowledge did, based on a runtime test it can reason about.
3ddd1f4962: 15. Why does the second list(gen) return []? A generator is a single-use iterator. The first list() drives it to exhaustion, and there's no rewind. The generator function can be called again to make a fresh generator. But the generator object is spent. If you need the data twice, materialize it into a list once.
5fe673d767: 16. What does yield from give you that a manual for loop doesn't? Delegation. yield from subgen() yields every value from the sub-generator. It also passes the sub-generator's return value back as the expression's value. A manual loop drops the return value on the floor. yield from also forwards send()/throw() into the sub-generator, which a loop can't do.
9c08b835bc: 17. If the body of a with block raises, does cleanup still run? What if __exit__ returns a true value? Yes. That's the entire point of context managers: __exit__ runs on the exception path too. If __exit__ returns a truthy value, it suppresses the exception, and the with statement exits normally. A falsy return re-raises it. Suppress deliberately and rarely. Swallowing exceptions silently is a debugging nightmare.
fb474e8ccb: 18. What's wrong with wrapping a large block in except Exception: pass? It hides every failure, including bugs you haven't thought of: NameError from a typo, KeyboardInterrupt (well, that's BaseException), real logic errors. You lose the traceback. The program continues in a state you can't reason about, and the bug surfaces far from its cause. Catch what you can actually handle, as narrowly as possible, and let the rest propagate.
57d60d5b85: 19. Why write raise StoreError(...) from exc instead of a bare raise StoreError(...)? Chaining preserves the causal chain. With from exc, the traceback shows both the original error (the JSONDecodeError) and the higher-level one, with "directly caused by" between them. A bare re-raise leaves you guessing what the low-level failure was. Chaining keeps the evidence.
7c1e6d2c43: 20. Module a imports b, and b imports a, and you get an ImportError on a partially initialized module. What's happening, and what's the standard fix? Python executes a module's top-level code on first import. a starts importing b, and b starts importing a. At that point a is only half-executed, so the names b wants don't exist yet. There are two fixes. Move one import inside the function that needs it, deferring it until call time. Or restructure so the shared names live in a third module both import.
fae1584536: 21. CPU-bound number crunching: threads, processes, or asyncio? Why? Processes. In standard CPython the GIL lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time. So threads can't parallelize CPU work. (They help with I/O-bound work, where threads wait while others run.) asyncio is single-threaded cooperation: great for many waiting connections, useless for computation. Processes each get their own interpreter and GIL, so they genuinely run in parallel. The price is heavier startup and explicit data passing.
8ef481edb1: 22. What does await actually do to the event loop? It suspends the current coroutine and returns control to the loop. The loop runs other ready coroutines until the awaited thing completes. Nothing blocks: one thread, many tasks taking turns. That's why await inside a coroutine is cheap. Calling a blocking function (like time.sleep) inside one freezes everything, because it never yields.
29052c821d: 23. Why is pickle.loads on untrusted data a security hole? Unpickling isn't just reading data. It can construct arbitrary objects and call callables during loading. A crafted pickle payload executes attacker code on loads. Never unpickle data you didn't produce. For untrusted input, use json or another format that only builds plain data.
370108f8b6: 24. Same question for eval on user input. eval executes its argument as Python code with your program's privileges. "User input" becomes "user's program running inside yours," with file access, imports, everything. If you need to parse user-supplied data, use json.loads or ast.literal_eval. The latter only builds literals and never executes.
8b521a6515: Every topic promised in the guide's scope is verified present here. Sections map to chapters in order. Chapter 5 carries both dataclasses and type hints. Chapter 6 carries iteration together with errors, modules, and everyday tooling. Chapter 7 is the testing and concurrency chapter.
